claims.text: Dermatology AI fails in dark-skin, non-cancer settings.
claims.poster_quote: Dermatology AI fails in dark-skin, non-cancer settings.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Patients present with more pigmented skin, and with a disease burden dominated by inflammatory and infectious conditions (eczema, tinea, impetigo, scabies) that are largely absent from cancer-centric training data.
claims.reason: Section 1 Introduction explicitly states that dermatology AI models trained on light-skinned, cancer-focused data fail in settings with darker skin and non-cancerous conditions like eczema or tinea.

claims.text: Disease shift may matter more than skin tone underrepresentation.
claims.poster_quote: Disease shift may matter more than skin tone underrepresentation.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: If the dominant driver is disease distribution, tone-diversification alone will not close the gap. Distribution shift is a known failure mode for medical AI [...] dermatology is especially challenging because tone and disease prevalence shift simultaneously, obscuring the cause of failure.
claims.reason: Section 1 Introduction discusses how disease distribution may be a more significant factor than skin tone underrepresentation in the generalization gap.

claims.text: Models trained on light-skinned, cancer-focused data are deployed where patients have darker skin and non-cancerous conditions like eczema or tinea.
claims.poster_quote: Models trained on light-skinned, cancer-focused data are deployed where patients have darker skin and non-cancerous conditions like eczema or tinea.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Artificial intelligence (AI) models are trained predominantly on light-skinned, cancer-focused image collections, yet are increasingly proposed for deployment in resource-constrained settings (RCS) whose patients differ from the training population along two confounded axes at once: skin tone and disease distribution.
claims.reason: Abstract explicitly states that models trained on light-skinned, cancer-focused data are deployed in settings with darker skin and non-cancerous conditions.

claims.text: Distribution shift causes bigger drops than tone gaps.
claims.poster_quote: Distribution shift causes bigger drops than tone gaps.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: In our setting, disease-distribution shift contributes more than skin tone: the cancer baseline degrades sharply from its in-domain performance to unfamiliar conditions (a drop from 0.62 to 0.21 balanced accuracy across clinical categories), a far larger effect than the within-disease skin-tone gap, which is comparatively small (0.10-0.18) and did not show a consistent direction.
claims.reason: Abstract and Table 2 confirm that distribution shift causes larger performance drops than tone gaps.

claims.text: Table 2 shows 0.62→0.21 drop for cancer baseline on SCIN.
claims.poster_quote: Table 2 shows 0.62→0.21 drop for cancer baseline on SCIN.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: In our setting, disease-distribution shift contributes more than skin tone: the cancer baseline degrades sharply from its in-domain performance to unfamiliar conditions (a drop from 0.62 to 0.21 balanced accuracy across clinical categories).
claims.reason: Abstract and Table 2 explicitly state the 0.62 to 0.21 drop for the cancer baseline on SCIN.

claims.text: Label-free analysis reveals cancer features collapse to near-chance on unfamiliar conditions (+0.06 purity lift).
claims.poster_quote: Label-free analysis reveals cancer features collapse to near-chance on unfamiliar conditions (+0.06 purity lift).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: On its home domain, the cancer baseline has the strongest representational structure of any model (purity lift +0.42), yet on SCIN its features barely separate conditions (+0.06) close to chance, demonstrating a genuine representational deficit rather than a missing output head.
claims.reason: Section 4.2 and Figure 2 confirm that the cancer baseline's features collapse to near-chance on unfamiliar conditions, with a +0.06 purity lift.

claims.text: Dermatology models retain transferable structure (DermLIP +0.23).
claims.poster_quote: while dermatology models retain transferable structure (DermLIP +0.23).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Dermatology foundation models retain three to four times more transferable structure under the same unfamiliar conditions (DermLIP +0.23).
claims.reason: Section 4.2 and Figure 2 confirm that dermatology models retain transferable structure, with DermLIP achieving a +0.23 purity lift.

claims.text: Representation quality strongly correlates with recoverable performance (r=0.90).
claims.poster_quote: Representation quality strongly correlates with recoverable performance (r=0.90).
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Across models, recoverable performance closely tracks the label-free representation quality of Fig. 2 (r = 0.90 between SCIN purity lift and full-probe balanced accuracy across the four models).
claims.reason: Section 4.3 explicitly states that representation quality strongly correlates with recoverable performance (r=0.90).

claims.text: Use dermatology foundation models, not cancer ones.
claims.poster_quote: Use dermatology foundation models, not cancer ones.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: First, model selection may matter more than local retraining: since recoverable performance is bounded by representation quality, teams may benefit from starting with a dermatology-pretrained foundation model rather than a cancer-specialized classifier.
claims.reason: Section 6 Impact in Resource-Constrained Settings explicitly recommends using dermatology foundation models over cancer-specialized ones.

claims.text: Adapt with 10 examples/class; runs on CPU.
claims.poster_quote: Adapt with 10 examples/class; runs on CPU.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Second, modest labeling may suffice: a few-shot probe with roughly ten labeled examples per local category recovered most attainable performance in our experiments, suggesting a clinic could adapt a model with a small, locally curated label set. [...] Finally, [...] the adaptation step itself is lightweight and runs on CPU, so the main hardware demand falls on the one-time feature extraction rather than on repeated local training.
claims.reason: Section 6 Impact in Resource-Constrained Settings confirms that adaptation with 10 examples per class is possible and runs on CPU.

claims.text: Table 3 confirms recovery.
claims.poster_quote: Table 3 confirms recovery.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Table 3. Low-compute adaptation on SCIN categories (balanced accuracy). Few-shot uses 10 examples/class. Recovery tracks latent structure (Fig. 2); the cancer baseline cannot be cheaply rescued.
claims.reason: Table 3 confirms recovery results for few-shot adaptation.

claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For each (model, dataset) pair we extract frozen embeddings and evaluate with three analyses. (1) Linear probing. [...] (2) Label-free representation quality. [...] (3) Low-compute adaptation.
claims.reason: Section 3.3 Evaluation Protocol explicitly describes testing four frozen models on two datasets using linear probing, kNN, and few-shot adaptation.

claims.text: Fig. 1 shows the pipeline.

claims.reason: Figure 1 shows the pipeline as described in the claim.

claims.text: Models include cancer-trained ResNet-50, dermatology foundation models (DermLIP, MONET), and general vision model DINOv3.
claims.poster_quote: Models include cancer-trained ResNet-50, dermatology foundation models (DermLIP, MONET), and general vision model DINOv3.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We evaluate four models as frozen feature extractors: (i) a cancer baseline, ResNet-50 (ImageNet-initialized) fine-tuned on the pooled HAM10000+ISIC eight-class task, with the classification head removed to yield 2048-d features; (ii) DermLIP [4] (512-d) and (iii) MONET [5] (1024-d), open dermatology vision-language foundation models; and (iv) DINOv3 [13] (facebook/dinov3-vitb16-pretrain-lvd1689m, pooler output, 768-d), a general-purpose self-supervised vision model pretrained on natural images.
claims.reason: Section 3.2 Models explicitly lists the four models evaluated, including the cancer-trained ResNet-50, dermatology foundation models (DermLIP, MONET), and general vision model DINOv3.
